items.title: Police arrest 25-year-old man over attempted armed robbery in Ashanti Region
items.description: Police in the Ashanti Region have arrested a 25-year-old man in connection with an alleged attempted armed robbery on the Hiakose-Newense stretch in the Manso Nkwanta District. The suspect, identified as Francis Nsiah, was arrested after he sought medical attention for a gunshot wound sustained during the incident on Friday, August 7, 2026. According to the Nkawie Divisional Police Command, its operations patrol team received information at about 11pm that an armed robbery was underway along the Hiakose-Newense road. Officers who responded to the distress call heard gunshots as they approached the area. The police said the officers spotted one of the suspected robbers fleeing into a nearby bush with a bag and pursued him, while a subsequent search of the area led to the recovery of an iPhone 14 and a bag believed to belong to some of the victims. The police later received information that one of the suspected robbers had reported to a medical facility for treatment after sustaining a gunshot injury. Officers proceeded to the facility, where they arrested Nsiah. He was found to have suffered a gunshot wound to the left side of his buttock and is currently receiving medical treatment under police guard. The Nkawie Divisional Police Command said investigations were ongoing to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident and identify and arrest other suspects believed to have been involved.

items.title: Gov’t must prioritise essential services amid debt pressures – Veep Opoku-Agyemang
items.description: Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang has defended the government’s approach to public spending, saying Ghana’s significant debt obligations require difficult choices and careful prioritisation of limited resources. Speaking on the KSM Show on Friday, August 7, 2026, Prof. Opoku-Agyemang said government could not meet every public demand at a time when the country was saddled with substantial debt. She said while some obligations could be renegotiated, others had to be settled, making it necessary for government to focus on areas that provide broad benefits to citizens. “If you decide that where we are as a country is not an easy place, and we owe many people, then you must prioritise. Some debts can be renegotiated, while others must be paid,” she said. She cautioned that spreading available resources too thinly for political popularity could undermine essential sectors such as healthcare, education and infrastructure. The Vice President said the ultimate test of government’s performance should be whether citizens experience tangible improvements in their daily lives. She pointed to improved roads, access to healthcare and measures that ease the financial burden on families supporting children in school as examples of interventions that could benefit citizens regardless of their political affiliation. “Ultimately, people want results. They want outcomes they can see and feel,” she said.

items.title: Mir Raza’s grave is not a silent one
items.description: There is a particular cruelty in a name being spoken twice by death. Once when it is buried. And once when it is dug up again, because the truth could not rest with it. Mir Raza, the son of Mir Hassan Ali Khan, and Wafflix business owner, was laid into the earth of Rehorania Masjid graveyard on the 29th of July. Eleven days later, a board of doctors, a police surgeon, a magistrate, and a family that refused to let silence be the final word stood over that same soil and opened it again. I have read the report. I do not think I will ever be able to unread it. It is written in the flat, careful language that medicine keeps for what it cannot otherwise bear to say. Somewhere inside that distance is a twenty-five-year-old man who once had a face his mother could recognise without being told his name. What the doctors found confirmed what the family had feared all along, that Mir Raza did not simply die. He was taken from them. And when asked, plainly, whether his wounds came before death, someone circled a single word on the page: Yes . That word has not left me since. What stays with me most is not the injury itself, but the effort that surrounded it. The care taken. The insistence, even now, that this body still deserved to be handled gently, named properly, treated as someone rather than something. Dr Summaiya Syed, Police Surgeon of Karachi, stood at that graveside and did what very few of us are ever asked to do. She looked directly at what injustice leaves behind, and she did not turn away. There is a particular kind of courage in choosing, on an ordinary working day, to be the last honest witness a murdered man will ever have. It is not the courage of headlines. It is quieter than that, and heavier, and it asks everything of the stomach and the soul, and gives back only the satisfaction of having told the truth when it would have been so much easier not to. And yet, the final word on how Mir Raza died has still not been given. Not because there is doubt. The findings speak clearly enough. It has simply not been said out loud, in the way that matters, in the place that matters. Twelve days passed, the doctors believe, between his death and the moment anyone was able to examine him. Twelve days in which a family did not know. And then more days still, in which even his grave had to be argued for, before the truth was allowed to be looked at a second time. We spend our lives pretending we are not what that grave revealed. We make plans, we argue over small things, we behave as though we will always have tomorrow to fix what we said today. But strip away the years, and every one of us ends the same way Mir Raza did. Plain. Unrecognisable, even to those who loved us most. If that is where we are all headed, then what exactly are we fighting for when we fight for justice? I do not think it is the body. The earth takes that regardless. I think it is the truth of what was done to someone while they were still here to feel it. That is the only part of us that does not decay. It is the only inheritance a murdered man can leave behind that no grave is deep enough to bury. Karachi did not let this one go quiet. Somewhere between a graveyard and a courtroom, ordinary people, neighbours, strangers, a city that has buried too many of its sons without asking enough questions, decided that Mir Raza’s silence was not going to be mistaken for peace. They spoke. They kept speaking, until an order was signed and a grave that should have been the end of his story became instead the place where it finally began to be told properly. That is not a small thing. In a country where so many cases are allowed to fade as quietly as a body returns to the earth, the refusal of ordinary citizens to look away is very often the only justice the dead will ever be given. So I find myself asking the only question I have left. If the truth has already been found, plainly, and written down, and confirmed by a circled word on a page, then what are we still waiting for? Where does justice go, in the space between a death and its acknowledgment? And where, in a city that loved this man loudly enough to bring him back up into the light so his story could be told rightly, does our humanity actually stand today? Not in the vigils. Not in the slogans. But in the quiet, unglamorous work of finishing what we started for Mir Raza. I do not have that answer yet. I am not sure any of us do. But I know this much. A city that will not let its dead be forgotten has not yet forgotten itself. And whatever else remains unresolved, that much still holds true: somewhere beneath all our exhaustion and all our grief, we still believe a man’s name is worth saying twice. Header image: Mir Raza Ali, a 25-year-old business owner whose body was found in bushes in Karachi’s Gulistan-i-Jauhar on July 29, following which a police probe into his death is ongoing. — Instagram/Wafflix

items.title: GoldBod to support reclamation of three devastated forest reserves in 2027 – Sammy Gyamfi
items.description: The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) will support the reclamation of three forest reserves affected by illegal mining next year as part of efforts to restore degraded landscapes, its Chief Executive Officer, Sammy Gyamfi, has disclosed. Mr Gyamfi said GoldBod had already commenced supporting reclamation activities in some affected areas, including the Tano Nimri Forest Reserve, while Apaprama was also expected to benefit from the intervention. He explained that the initiative was being undertaken despite GoldBod not being responsible for the destruction of the forest reserves, stressing that the institution had a responsibility to contribute to the broader national effort to combat the environmental consequences of illegal mining. Speaking during a Space conversation on X on Sunday, August 9, Mr Gyamfi said, “We are reclaiming it. And next year, we are taking up three devastated forest reserves because the President is so passionate about it; it is dear to his heart, and says GoldBod, you need to help in this fight.” He said GoldBod’s environmental interventions were being pursued alongside efforts to formalise small-scale mining, improve traceability and promote responsible mining practices. “The solving of environmental concerns while at the same time dealing with the economic need that the gold must meet are not mutually exclusive; it goes hand in hand,” he said. Mr Gyamfi also disclosed that GoldBod had provided GH¢5 million and five pickup vehicles to the National Inter-Ministerial Committee on Illegal Mining (NAIMOS) to support its enforcement operations. He added that the Board had budgeted for 10 speedboats to strengthen efforts to tackle illegal mining on water bodies, noting that the boats had already been ordered and were being manufactured. The GoldBod CEO urged Ghanaians to give the interventions time to deliver results, arguing that the country’s illegal mining crisis had developed over several years and could not be resolved overnight. He said a combination of formalisation, enforcement, reclamation and gold traceability would be necessary to reduce the environmental damage caused by illegal mining while ensuring that Ghana derives maximum economic value from its gold resources.

items.title: Poor formalisation of small-scale mining worsened galamsey crisis – GoldBod CEO
items.description: The Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), Sammy Gyamfi, has attributed Ghana’s persistent illegal mining crisis partly to decades of inadequate formalisation and state support for artisanal and small-scale mining. He said although Ghana began formalising the sector in 1989, successive governments failed to provide sufficient training, equipment, monitoring and environmental safeguards to make small-scale mining sustainable. Mr Gyamfi said the problem was also worsened by the dominance of private operators in the domestic gold-buying sector, which, he argued, made it difficult for the state to effectively track the source of gold being purchased from miners. He questioned whether previous government-backed gold-buying initiatives had adequate mechanisms to determine whether the gold being purchased was sourced from legitimate mining operations. Speaking during a Space conversation on X on Sunday, August 9, Mr Gyamfi said, “Very little was done to provide formalisation support, training, capacity building, and investing in reclamation.” He also questioned the traceability arrangements under the previous government’s Domestic Gold Purchase Programme, which was introduced in 2021 to support the purchase of gold for reserves, foreign exchange and the Gold for Oil programme. “When government decided to go into gold purchases in 2021 under the Domestic Gold Purchase Programme, they were doing gold for oil, they were doing gold for reserves, they were doing gold for forex,” he said. “But did you ever hear there was traceability under the ex-government? Did you ever hear an effort, even an effort to ensure that the gold they were buying for oil, gold for reserve, gold for forex was traceable?” he asked. Mr Gyamfi said Ghana also failed to establish adequate systems to register and monitor mining equipment, geofence mining operations and track activities across mining areas. He argued that the absence of a comprehensive traceability framework had made it difficult to determine whether gold purchased by the state originated from licensed operations or environmentally destructive illegal mining activities.

items.title: La France et l’Europe deviendront-elles inassurables ?
items.description: Les sécheresses exceptionnelles et les incendies qui ont frappé la France, l’Espagne et une grande partie de l’Europe cet été auront des conséquences économiques majeures, dont on commence seulement à mesurer l’ampleur : destruction de logements et de capital productif, pertes de production colossales, notamment dans l’agriculture et l’industrie agroalimentaire, suivie par une inflation importante sur les prix de ces produits. Selon les données rassemblées par l’Agence européenne de l’environnement, les quatre années 2021-2024 ont été celles où les pertes économiques directes causée par des événements climatiques (tempêtes, inondations, incendies, gel, grêle et sécheresse) ont été les plus importantes depuis 1980, avec 208 milliards d’euros de dommages recensés pour l’ensemble de l’Union. Lorsque les données de 2026 seront également disponibles, ce record sera, selon toute probabilité, largement dépassé. Ces événements, désormais récurrents et dont l'impact est croissant d'année en année, posent de très nombreuses questions en matière de politiques publiques d'adaptation au changement climatique. Ils créent notamment de graves difficultés pour le secteur des assurances, qui est l'un des moyens privilégiés depuis longtemps pour amortir le choc provoqué par ce type d'événements pour des individus, des régions ou des activités donnés. Or, la fréquence croissante des événements climatiques extrêmes et la hausse des coûts qu’ils engendrent mettent les assureurs à mal. Il s'agit en plus de dynamiques nouvelles et changeantes, pour lesquelles ils ne disposent pas de l’historique nécessaire pour estimer les risques et ajuster les primes d’assurance dans les cas usuels. En réaction, ils ont tendance à augmenter fortement leurs tarifs et/ou à réduire leur couverture. Ce qui revient à laisser de plus en plus de citoyens et d'entreprises assumer seuls ces coûts. Cette tendance est d'autant plus préoccupante que, selon la Banque centrale européenne The climate insurance protection gap », Banque centrale européenne.'> 1 et le régulateur européen des assurances, seuls un quart des dommages causés par les événements climatiques sont actuellement couverts par les assureurs dans l'Union. Dans un contexte où le montant de ces pertes explose d’année en année, les Européens ont certainement besoin de plus de couverture assurantielle, et non de moins. Or, c'est précisément dans cette direction que la dynamique spontanée du marché conduit les acteurs Dashboard on insurance protection gap for natural catastrophes », European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority.'> 2 . Outre les problèmes humains, sociaux et économiques colossaux que cela engendre, ces pertes non assurées créent également des risques supplémentaires pour l'autre pilier du système financier : les banques. Celles-ci se retrouvent en effet confrontées à des clients, particuliers ou entreprises, incapables de rembourser les crédits qu’elles leur ont accordés, comme le rappelle le Center for Economic Transition Expertise de la London School of Economics The insurance–bank nexus : the climate protection gap as a source of risk for the financial system », CETEX, 25 juin 2026.'> 3 . Si la question des pertes non assurées n'est pas réglée, les banques risquent de refuser des crédits ou d'augmenter fortement leurs taux pour des clients, des régions ou des secteurs jugés à risque, ce qui amplifiera les effets négatifs des événements climatiques. C'est la raison pour laquelle, depuis 2023, la Banque centrale européenne et le régulateur européen des assurances appellent ensemble à la création d'un mécanisme européen de réassurance — une assurance des assurances en quelque sorte –, pour les risques liés au climat. Ce dispositif pourrait être complété par la création d'un fonds public européen pour aider les États membres à faire face à ces risques pour les infrastructures publiques. La mise en place de mécanismes de ce type ne peut et ne doit évidemment pas servir à maintenir le statu quo et se substituer à une politique d’adaptation volontariste au changement climatique. C’est le problème classique de l’aléa moral en matière d’assurances : en limitant les coûts subis suite à tel ou tel sinistre, on limite aussi l’incitation à prendre des mesures pour éviter que le problème ne se reproduise à l’avenir. Pour éviter cela, des mesures européennes de réassurance au profit des États membres pourraient être conditionnées à la mise en place effective de plans d’adaptation ambitieux. L’article La France et l’Europe deviendront-elles inassurables ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Ghana Exim Bank commissions astro turf park in Anloga
items.description: Ghana Exim Bank has commissioned a newly constructed astro turf facility at Hogbe Park in Anloga in the Volta Region as part of activities marking its 10th anniversary. The project forms part of the Bank’s Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives aimed at promoting youth empowerment and community development. The ultra-modern facility, built to international standards, has been named the Awoamefia Togbui Sri III Astro Turf Park in honour of the Overlord of Anlo State in recognition of his role in facilitating the project. Mr Sylvester Adinam Mensah, Deputy Chief Executive of Ghana Exim Bank, said at the commissioning ceremony that the completion of the facility marked a significant milestone in the Bank’s efforts to support community development. He noted that the project was not merely a ceremonial undertaking but a deliberate investment in a community that had long lacked a modern facility capable of supporting competitive football and organised sporting activities. Mr Mensah said the old Hogbe Park had served the community for decades, hosting football matches, social events and activities associated with the Hogbetsotso Festival, but had become inadequate as sporting standards evolved. He said the proposal for the astro turf project was carefully assessed by the Bank and found to be credible. “The old playing field, formerly known as Hogbe Park, holds decades of memory for the community, including games, events and gatherings, Hogbetsotso festival, had outgrown its usefulness as sporting standards evolved which necessitated the modern replacement,” he said. Mr Mensah explained that the facility would support year-round sporting activities regardless of weather conditions, reduce maintenance costs associated with natural grass pitches, and provide a suitable venue for training programmes, tournaments and inter-community competitions. He announced the establishment of a management committee to oversee the day-to-day operations of the facility, stressing that effective governance was essential to ensuring its sustainability. According to him, a well-managed sports facility could generate revenue, create employment opportunities for ground staff, administrators, security personnel and vendors, and attract visitors whose spending would contribute to the local economy. He said the facility would also provide the youth with a structured environment to develop their sporting talents. “The Ghana Exim Bank’s mandate extended beyond financing physical structures to fostering productive economic activity, a well-managed sports facility could generate revenue, create employment for groundkeepers, administrators, security personnel and vendors, and attract visiting teams and officials whose spending would benefit the local economy.” Mr Mensah added that the facility would also provide young people in Anloga with a structured, organised outlet for their sporting talents, adding that, “such interventions built discipline, foster positive association, and channelled youthful energy into productive pursuits.” Mr Mensah, however, cautioned that the Bank’s commitment did not end with the commissioning, adding that Ghana Exim Bank would continue to monitor the use of the facility. He expressed the expectation that the management committee would maintain proper records and ensure responsible access to preserve the facility for future generations. In a remark, Togbui Sri III on behalf of the chiefs, queen mothers and people of Anlo Dukor, expressed gratitude to the Board, Management and staff of Ghana Exim Bank for selecting Anloga to benefit from the CSR project. He described the facility as a transformative development that had turned the old park into a modern recreational centre where young people could nurture their sporting talents and aspire to excel in sports. Togbui Sri III commended all stakeholders who contributed to the successful completion of the project and pledged, together with the traditional leadership, to ensure its proper maintenance. Madam Sandra Seyram Kpedor, District Chief Executive for Anloga, described the astro turf project as a major investment in youth development, sports and community growth. She expressed confidence that the facility would provide a platform for young people to develop their talents and pursue their aspirations. The Bank also expressed appreciation to the Ministry of Sports and Recreation, regional and district authorities, contractors, technical personnel and the people of Anloga for their support during the implementation of the project. Some residents who spoke to the Ghana News Agency thanked the Bank for the initiative and commended Mr Mensah, a native of the area, for his contribution towards bringing the project to Anlo. The colourful ceremony was attended by Togbi Agbesi Awusu II, Awadada of Anlo, other chiefs and queen mothers of the Anlo Traditional Council, officials of Ghana Exim Bank, representatives of the Anloga and Keta Municipal Assemblies, and invited guests.

items.title: 3rd phase of AJK polls: Voting underway in Poonch Division's Bagh and Haveli districts
items.description: The third phase of elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) is currently underway in four constituencies in Poonch Division’s Bagh and Haveli districts. Polling began at 8am and will continue until 5pm. Government officials have anticipated clashes in some areas, while the Election Commission has classified most of the 803 polling stations in the four constituencies as either sensitive or highly sensitive. “Apart from the regular police of both districts, we have dispatched an additional 10,300 troops to maintain law and order and provide a fear-free atmosphere to voters,” Election Commission Secretary Raja Mohammad Shakeel told Dawn earlier. Elections are being held across AJK in phases amid tensions between protesters and the authorities. Polling in Mirpur and Muzaff­arabad divisions was held on July 27 and Aug 2, respectively, with the PML-N securing 24 seats. The PPP has only secured 10 seats so far. The third phase of the polls was originally meant to cover all of Poonch Division. The division comprises 11 constituencies, including three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district. However, last week the AJK Election Commission announced that polling would only go ahead as scheduled in Bagh and Haveli due to concerns over the law and order situation. The AJK election commissioner has hinted that polling on the remaining seven constituencies could be held by Aug 20 or 21. Rathore, two ex-AJK PMs face crucial electoral test AJK Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore and two of his predecessors — Sardar Tanveer Ilyas and Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan — face a battle for political survival as voters head to the polls. Around 238,664 men and 221,707 women are eligible to cast their ballots at 803 polling stations comprising 1,254 polling booths. A total of 82 candidates are in the fray, with LA-14 (Dhirkot) attracting the highest number of candidates at 30 and LA-17 (Haveli) the lowest at nine. In LA-17, Rathore is facing PML-N candidate Engr Mohsin Aziz and independent candidate Khawaja Tariq Saeed, a member of the AJK Council. Rathore and Saeed had been political allies and, under an agreement, had agreed to contest the seat alternately. However, after becoming prime minister, Rathore asked Saeed to step aside in his favour, a request he did not accept, turning the former allies into rivals. Aziz, whose father, Chaudhry Mohammad Aziz, had won the seat at least three times, draws support from the sizeable Gujjar community. His recent large election rally in Forward Kahuta reportedly surprised his rivals and underscored the strength of his campaign. Saeed, meanwhile, is believed to enjoy the backing of a sizeable section of the Kashmiri community, as well as an alliance of several smaller clans. Rathore, however, remains confident of retaining the seat, citing the performance of his government during his relatively brief tenure as prime minister. The constituency has also witnessed allegations of electoral irregularities on social media, with reports claiming that two presiding officers had been caught manipulating results in favour of Rathore. Shakeel dismissed the allegations but at the same time confirmed that complaints had been received against the two officials and that they had subsequently been relieved of election duties. In LA-15 (Wasti Bagh), former prime minister Ilyas is facing PML-N candidate and former minister Mushtaq Ahmed Minhas, PPP nominee and sitting minister Sardar Ziaul Qamar, and Jamaat-i-Islami candidate retired Brig Dr Mohammad Khan, a respected educationist. Ilyas, who secured a little over 3,300 votes from Upper Neelum in the second phase of the elections, had initially announced a boycott of the third phase. He subsequently reversed the decision and resumed campaigning, claiming that his victory would enable the constituency to “secure either the presidency or prime ministership.” Ilyas and Qamar belong to the same Madiyal tribe, while Brig Khan belongs to the Narma clan and enjoys the support of former JI chief Abdul Rashid Turabi and former adviser Raja Yasin Khan. Minhas has the advantage of belonging to the PML-N, which is poised to form the next government after emerging as the largest party in the elections held so far. His campaign has also stressed the argument that voters should elect a candidate from the party that is set to occupy the government benches rather than send their representative to the opposition. In LA-16 (Sharqi Bagh), former ministers Sardar Mir Akbar and Sardar Qamar Zaman are the principal contenders, representing the PML-N and PPP, respectively. The fourth contest, LA-14 (Dhirkot), has drawn particular attention because of the challenge faced by Sardar Attique, head of the once-dominant Muslim Conference (MC). Attique is reportedly facing a strong challenge from Sajid Iqbal Abbasi of the relatively new Awam Dast-o-Bazu Party. A contractor and philanthropist, Abbasi is said to have spent millions of rupees from his own resources on public welfare projects in the constituency, helping him build a sizeable personal following. Attique, who has represented the constituency successively since 2006, when he first became prime minister, faces an additional challenge in that Abbasi also belongs to the same tribe. Among nearly two dozen other candidates are PML-N’s nominee Raja Faisal Azad and PPP candidate Raja Mubashar Ejaz. While the main contest is seen as being between Attique and Abbasi, the PML-N and PPP nominees are expected to vie for the second runner-up position.

items.title: Veep Opoku-Agyemang bids farewell to outgoing Brazilian Ambassador
items.description: Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang has bid farewell to Madam Mariana Gonçalves Madeira, the outgoing Brazilian Ambassador to Ghana. A statement issued by the Office of the Vice President said Prof Opoku-Agyemang, on behalf of President John Dramani Mahama and the Government and people of Ghana, thanked Madam Madeira for her service to strengthening relations between the two countries. The Vice President noted that the relationship between Ghana and Brazil extended far beyond contemporary diplomacy. She said the two countries shared deep historical and cultural ties shaped by the movement of people across the Atlantic, adding that these connections continued to be reflected in their cultures today. Prof Opoku-Agyemang said the shared experiences of the two nations provided a strong foundation for partnerships that delivered tangible benefits to their peoples. She said discussions with the Ambassador covered cooperation in agriculture and agribusiness, energy, security and defence, trade, and other areas of mutual interest. The Vice President particularly welcomed opportunities for increased collaboration in the energy sector, including through Petrobras, as Ghana sought to expand its energy capacity and attract strategic investment. She also acknowledged Brazil’s partnership with Ghana on important international initiatives, including efforts related to the historic United Nations resolution on the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade, as well as cooperation within the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty and other programmes focused on women and social development. Prof Opoku-Agyemang commended Madam Madeira for going beyond the formal requirements of diplomacy through her engagement with various stakeholders in Ghana, notably the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, the Ga Traditional Council, and initiatives supporting food security and social development. As the Ambassador departs Ghana, the Vice President wished her success in the next chapter of her diplomatic career. She said Ghana looked forward to working with her successor to sustain the momentum and further strengthen bilateral relations between the two countries. For her part, Madam Madeira reflected on the progress she had witnessed in Ghana and commended the President and Government for efforts to strengthen the economy. She described Ghana as an important partner of Brazil and expressed confidence in the potential for both countries to deepen cooperation in areas of mutual benefit.

items.title: Nigeria’s economy recovering after painful reforms —NRS
items.description: ABUJA — The Nigeria Revenue Service, NRS, has said the Nigerian economy is showing strong signs of recovery and accelerated growth following a series of “painful” reforms implemented by President Bola Tinubu. The revenue service, in an internal report, said the economy had moved “decisively from acute macroeconomic distress toward a more stable and increasingly resilient footing.” According to the report, the improvement followed reforms introduced by the Tinubu administration. The NRS said the administration inherited four major economic distortions: a fiscally unsustainable fuel subsidy regime, an opaque foreign exchange system that discouraged investment, a non-performing oil sector and a tax base “far below its potential.” It said that despite the initial economic pains associated with the reforms, key indicators were now pointing to recovery, including retreating inflation, an improved balance of payments, increased oil production, higher tax collections and changes in the country’s productive base. The report said minimum wage had doubled between 2023 and 2026, while policies and incentives introduced by the government had contributed to reducing the number of out-of-school children from 20 million to 18.3 million, according to UNICEF estimates. It also credited the naira-for-crude arrangement with Dangote Refinery and other local refineries with helping Nigeria become a net exporter of petroleum products after decades of dependence on imports. Oil production, according to the report, rose from about 1.2–1.3 million barrels per day in 2023 to 1.73 million barrels per day by July 2026, representing 104 per cent of the country’s OPEC quota. The NRS said the improved economic outlook had also been reflected in the capital market, with the market capitalisation of the Nigerian Exchange, NGX, rising from N30.36 trillion in 2023 to N161 trillion in 2026. It attributed the rally partly to improved macroeconomic credibility, banking-sector recapitalisation and a growing pool of domestic institutional investment. Tax collections more than doubled from N12.3 trillion in 2023 to N27.1 trillion as of July 2026, which the report attributed to the digitisation of tax systems, four new tax reform laws, transformation of the revenue service and an executive order aimed at closing loopholes. The report said economic growth increased from 2.74 per cent in 2023 to 3.8 per cent in the first half of 2026, while external reserves rose from $3.99 billion in 2023 to $51.9 billion as of July 2026. It added that the balance of payments moved from a $3.34 billion deficit to a $2.38 billion surplus in the first quarter of 2026. Nigeria’s trade position also improved, with the country moving from a marginal trade surplus of about N44.7 billion to N7.55 trillion in the first quarter of 2026. Annual capital importation increased from $3.9 billion in 2023 to $23.22 billion in 2025, while inflows reached $10.37 billion in the first quarter of 2026. The report also highlighted developments in the compressed natural gas, CNG, programme, saying more than 100,000 vehicles had reportedly been converted by 2026, with over $2 billion in investment mobilised and more than 10,000 jobs created. On agriculture, the NRS said federal agricultural allocation increased from N228.4 billion in 2023 to N826.5 billion in the 2025 budget, following measures including the release of strategic grain reserves, establishment of a N100 billion National Agricultural Development Fund, fertiliser distribution and agricultural mechanisation. The report said food prices had fallen by about 50 per cent by March 2026, citing the Ministry of Agriculture, but cautioned that agriculture would require several planting seasons for policy support to translate into increased output. On debt, the NRS said although Nigeria’s debt stock rose from N87.4 trillion in 2023 to N159.28 trillion in late 2025, the debt-to-GDP ratio fell from 38 per cent in 2023 to 35.5 per cent in 2025 and 32.3 per cent in 2026. It described the decline as the first sustained reduction in more than a decade, while debt servicing as a share of revenue fell from 68 per cent to an IMF-projected 53 per cent. The post Nigeria’s economy recovering after painful reforms —NRS appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Nigeria spent N3.1trn on domestic debt servicing in Q1 – DMO
items.description: The Debt Management Office, DMO, has said the federal government spent N3.14 trillion on servicing its domestic debt in the first quarter (Q1) of 2026. The office disclosed the data in its latest domestic debt service report for Q1 2026. The figure comprises N2.97 trillion in interest payments and N169.68 billion in principal repayments. The agency said in January, the government spent N741.82 billion on domestic debt service, while the figure rose to N967.67 billion in February. Debt service increased further to N1.43 trillion in March, bringing the total for the quarter to N3.14 trillion. The March figure was 47.7 percent higher than the N967.67 billion recorded in February and 92.7 percent above the N741.82 billion spent in January. Also, the debt office said interest payments accounted for about 94.6 percent of total domestic debt service during the quarter. The DMO said treasury bills accounted for the largest share of interest payments at N1 trillion, while interest on federal government bonds stood at N1.96 trillion. The agency said the government also paid N4.24 billion in interest on FGN savings bonds during the period. The DMO said the principal component of the debt service comprised N169.68 billion in repayments on local-denominated promissory notes. Overall, the government’s domestic debt service rose sharply through the quarter, with March accounting for almost half of the N3.14 trillion spent between January and March. Nigeria’s public debt increased by 0.01 percent to N159.35 trillion in the Q1 of 2026. On May 13, President Bola Tinubu said Nigeria would spend $11.6 billion on debt servicing in 2026. The post Nigeria spent N3.1trn on domestic debt servicing in Q1 – DMO appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Prime suspect in Rs8.5bn Yellow Line graft case under NAB scrutiny
items.description: KARACHI: The legal troubles of the prime suspect in the Rs8.5 billion Yellow Line graft case, Zameer Abbasi, have further increased as the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) has initiated an inquiry into his alleged possession of assets beyond his known sources of income and his alleged “illegal appointments” or “promotions in the Sindh government”. Earlier in June, the Anti-Corruption Establishment (ACE) Sindh had booked Abbasi, the then project director of the Karachi Mobility Project (KMP), and others following an inquiry into alleged financial mismanagement in the KMP related to the Yellow Line. The inquiry committee report stated that Abbasi and then director procurement Jhaman made Rs8.5bn advance payments to contractors without bank guarantees despite the fact that their contracts lacked any specific clause regarding “advance payment and financial assistance to the contractors”. A source told Dawn that the NAB had initiated an inquiry against the senior bureaucrat over allegations of possessing assets beyond his known sources of income and illegal appointments or promotions in the Sindh government. Bureau seeks details of Zameer Abbasi’s assets, ‘illegal’ appointments, promotions As part of the inquiry, the bureau has sought details of immovable properties registered in the names of Abbasi, his wife and children and other family members from the concerned departments. According to the source, Abbasi began his career with NAB and was later deputed to the Sindh police as a DSP. After a Supreme Court directive, he was repatriated to his parent department, the NAB, where he served until 2016. In the same year, he was appointed as a grade-17 section officer. The appointment was challenged before a court on allegations that it was made through irregularities and that he had also received an out-of-turn promotion, the source claimed. The source further alleged that Abbasi had also approached the court, contending that his colleagues who had joined service with him had already been promoted to grade 19. However, before the court could decide his petition, he was promoted to grade 19, the source claimed. In 2022, he was appointed to another key position, but the appointment was challenged before a court, which suspended the notification. Although he subsequently disappeared from the public spotlight for some time, he was later appointed to another important position, the source added. The ACE only managed to apprehend Abbasi, a grade-19 officer of the Sindh government, claiming that he was arrested in Lahore and later produced him before the court concerned in Karachi. The provincial anti-corruption court also rejected his post-arrest bail application. Published in Dawn, August 10th, 2026

items.title: Former MP urges tolerance, consensus as new Majority leadership takes shape in Parliament
items.description: Alex K. Agyekum, a former Member of Parliament (MP) for Mpohor, has called on Parliament to resist alleged growing tensions, intolerance, and political divisions following the change in Majority Leadership. In a statement issued on Sunday by Mr Agyekum to the Ghana News Agency, it warned “that the House must not descend into “chaos, confusion, and needless political confrontation.” The statement expressed concern that alleged commentary on social media was already creating divisions between the Majority and Minority caucuses. It cautioned that such narratives could undermine public confidence in the institution. “The incoming majority leader must remain focused on the constitutional mandate of Parliament and not be distracted by needless propaganda aimed at undermining the sanctity of the institution,” it said. The statement also urged Mr Alban Sumana Kingsford Bagbin, the Speaker of Parliament, and the leadership of Parliament to maintain neutrality and ensure that proceedings were conducted strictly in accordance with the Standing Orders and the Constitution. “Parliament must remain a place where laws are made and the activities of the executive are effectively scrutinised,” it stressed. Mr Agyekum noted that the need for tolerance and constructive engagement was particularly critical as Parliament prepared to consider the non-entrenched provisions of the Constitution recommended by the Constitution Review Committee. “Government has already issued a position paper on the matter,” it added. Mr Agyekum questioned whether a deeply polarised House, where the two caucuses were constantly at odds, could adequately debate such critical constitutional matters. “Can a Parliament where both sides are constantly at odds deliver the superior arguments and consensus required in the national interest?” he asked. To that end, Mr Ageykum challenged Mr James Agalga, the new Majority Leader, in his capacity as Leader of Government Business to prioritise building consensus across both sides of the House. “The focus should be on ensuring that the best constitutional amendment options are considered, rather than allowing Parliament to be dominated by acrimonious exchanges, entrenched positions, and boycotts,” the statement said. The statement further cautioned against what it described as an alleged growing social media narrative portraying an impending showdown between the two caucuses. It described such framing as counterproductive and urged leadership on both sides to prioritise “the dignity, stability, and constitutional responsibilities of Parliament” above partisan interests. Mr Agyekum was a former Chairman of the Youth and Sports Committee of Parliament and previously served on Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and the Education Committee during his tenure in Parliament.

items.title: Judicial probe launched into death of 2 girls in Lahore police custody
items.description: LAHORE: A judicial magistrate has initiated an inquiry under Section 176 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) into the suspicious death of two underage girls in Lahore police custody on Aug 4, as mystery continues to surround the horrific, tragic incident. The judicial inquiry was launched after the families of the victims – Amina and Anmol – demanded an impartial investigation into what happened to the girls in the police custody for well over two hours – from the time of their arrest to calling a Rescue 1122 team to the Township police station on Aug 4. Section 176 of the CrPC empowers a magistrate to inquire into the cause of death when a person dies in police custody or under some suspicious circumstances. The law also empowers the magistrate to order exhumation of a body for the postmortem examination, besides recording statements and examining witnesses on oath. Dawn spoke to police officers familiar with the matter and attempted to map the sequence of events from the girls’ arrest to their deaths. According to an official, around 2:54pm on Aug 4 an emergency call was received on police helpline 15 from complainant, Zeshan Latif, who alleged that two girls entered his house and fraudulently stole gold jewellery and cash belonging to his wife. A sub-inspector (SI) of the Township police, Ghulam Ghous, reached the scene at 3:11pm and brought the two girls to the police station, where they were handed over to the duty clerk (Muharrar), Tasnim Arif, at 3:26pm. Mr Latif subsequently submitted an application, which was e-tagged at 4:40pm, and an FIR was registered at 4:50pm against the two girls. The Township police station then recorded a report at 5:20pm regarding the transfer of the girls’ custody from the operations wing to the investigation staff. According to the official, the operations wing’s muharrar claimed that, following registration of the FIR, he handed over the girls to the investigation wing Muharrar Bilal, in accordance with the prescribed procedure. The situation took a grim turn shortly afterwards when, at 6:03pm, the central office of Rescue 1122 received an emergency call from the Township police regarding the deteriorating condition of both girls. A Rescue 1122 team reached the police station at 6:14pm and found one of the girls “almost dead”, while the other was unconscious, according to the official. Both were shifted to Jinnah Hospital, where doctors pronounced the unconscious girl dead. The other girl, who was reportedly in critical condition, also died shortly after in the hospital. As news of the girls’ death spread, senior police officers from the Saddar Division’s operations and investigation wings reached the Township police station at around 9:30pm and sensing gravity of the situation apprised higher authorities about the incident. The official says that incident triggered a row between the operations and investigation wings, with officers from both sides reportedly shifting the responsibility for the girls’ custody onto each other. The time between 3:11pm, when the girls were taken into custody, and 6:03pm, when Rescue 1122 was called, is therefore crucial in the judicial inquiry, he adds. Video footage that surfaced after the incident shows the girls apparently in a relatively stable condition when they were brought to the police station. In one recording, a police official can be seen questioning them. Another video recorded by a camera installed in the duty clerk’s room shows Amina and Anmol sitting on chairs inside the police station. They appear conscious and are seen interacting with the duty clerk before leaving the room. Police officials, however, say that details of the girls’ interaction and interrogation are not covered by the station’s security cameras. Immediately after the incident, the investigation police claimed that drug overdose was the likely cause of the girls’ death. The claim, however, has yet to be conclusively established through the postmortem reports, which are crucial evidence in determining the death cause. Police were still awaiting the final postmortem reports when Dawn spoke to officials. Investigation SSP Mohammad Naveed strongly rejected allegations that the girls had been tortured in custody. “Though I am not aware whether the final postmortem reports have been issued, I can assure you that the allegations of custodial torture are absolutely false and misleading,” he claimed. The SSP alleges that both girls were chronic drug users and had apparently consumed a strong addictive substance before being brought to the police station. “During their custody at the police station, they fainted, probably because of the impact of the drugs they had consumed, and later died of the same cause,” he claimed. Mr Naveed maintains that as a major portion of the girls interrogation had been captured by surveillance cameras installed at the police station, it shows girls were not maltreated in custody. He says the judicial inquiry had been initiated at the request of senior police officers under Section 176 of the CrPC and that its findings would bring out the circumstances of the deaths. Asked why the case had not been referred to the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), the SSP said the agency is usually asked to investigate the cases involving allegations that a suspect had died as a result of custodial torture or killed in a police encounter. “This case is different, as it concerns the deaths of two suspects in custody, and there was no need for an FIA investigation,” he insisted. The judicial inquiry is expected to examine the circumstances surrounding the girls’ detention, the transfer of their custody between the operations and investigation wings, the available CCTV footage, statements of police officials and witnesses, and the postmortem reports’ findings to dig out the facts. Published in Dawn, August 10th, 2026

items.title: Twifo Hemang SHTS appeals for administrative vehicle
items.description: Agnes Amoah, Headmistress of Twifo Hemang Senior High Technical School (SHTS), has appealed to the Government and other stakeholders to provide the school with an administrative vehicle to facilitate its operations. She made the appeal in an interview with the Ghana News Agency (GNA) at Twifo Hemang in the Twifo Hemang-Lower Denkyira District of the Central Region. Mrs Amoah said the absence of an official vehicle had become a major challenge for the school, compelling management to hire vehicles at a cost to transport examination materials to and from the District Education Directorate. She noted that the situation also affected the school’s ability to effectively participate in official programmes and ceremonies that required transportation. She said any activity that required the use of a vehicle places the school in a difficult situation and needed urgent attention. items.title: Only 6 banks pay N1.27trn dividends despite huge profits
items.description: ***t’s a conservative capital management strategy —CIS Boss ***CBN stopped the dividends —Adonri By Peter Egwuatu Only six of Nigeria’s biggest listed banks rewarded shareholders with a combined N1.27 trillion dividend for the 2025 financial year, while five other profitable lenders were barred from making payouts after failing to meet the Central Bank of Nigeria’s prudential requirements. Financial Vanguard findings showed that GTCO, Zenith Bank, Stanbic IBTC, Ecobank Transnational Incorporated, Wema Bank and FCMB passed the apex bank’s dividend eligibility test and declared payouts. However, five other banks, despite posting strong profits, withheld dividends as the CBN’s capital retention policy , rising non-performing loans and other prudential guidelines constrained their ability to reward share CBN’s prudential guidelines and rising Non-Performing Loans, NPLs, in many banks were responsible for the non-payment of dividend by the banks for the financial year ended 2025. Findings by Financial Vanguard showed that six banks paid dividends totaling N1.27 trillion to their shareholders, while five others did not pay, as they were unable to meet the dividend guideline set by the apex bank, even though they made profit. The banks that paid dividend include Guaranty Trust Bank, GTCO (N429.830 billion at N12.76 per share), Zenith Bank (N410.698 billion at N10.00 per share), Stanbic IBTC (N63.607 billion at N4.00 per share), Ecobank Transnational Incorporated ($40m at 0.16 cent per share); and FCMB (14.969 billion at 35kobo per share). The Tier-1 banks, which include GTCO and Zenith, accounted for the bulk of dividend payout, representing 81.9% Profit decline According to the audited financial statement ended December 31, 2025, the 11 big banks listed on the Exchange posted a combined Profit Before Tax (pretax) of N6.4 trillion against N6.7 trillion in the same period 2024, indicating a decline by 3.8%. The Tier-1 banks recorded N4.15 trillion pretax in 2025 against N5.06 trillion recorded in 2024, while Tier-2 posted N2.262 trillion against N1.602 trillion in 2024. Gross earnings The banks recorded combined gross earnings of N26.4 trillion in 2025 against N23.2 trillion in 2024. The Tier-1 banks’ gross earnings rose broadly, with the total amount collectively rising to N18.2 trillion from N16.9 trillion in the same period of 2024, while Tier-2 recorded N9.5 trillion from N7.6 trillion. The growth in gross earnings by the Tier-1 banks was led by Access Holdings recording N5.5 trillion in 2025 up from N4.9 trillion reported in 2024, while Zenith Bank followed with N4.1 trillion up from N3.8 trillion. GTCO saw its gross revenue rise slightly to N2.15 trillion in 2025 from N2.11 trillion in 2024. First HoldCo recorded an increase to N3.4 trillion against N3.2 trillion, while UBA recorded a slight decline to N2.97 trillion from N3.1 trillion. Analysts /Experts give insight Speaking to Financial Vanguard on the reasons some banks were unable to pay dividends, even when they made strong profit, Fiona Ahimie, President, Chartered Institute Stockbrokers, CIS said: “The divergence in dividend payments among Nigerian banks this year was primarily driven by differences in capital strength, regulatory compliance, earnings quality and strategic priorities, rather than profitability alone. ”Some banks declared dividends because they maintained strong capital adequacy ratios, delivered robust earnings and were able to satisfy regulatory requirements while retaining sufficient capital to support future growth. ”Others, despite reporting profits, opted not to pay dividends because preserving capital became a higher priority. ”This was influenced by the banking sector’s recapitalisation, the need to strengthen balance sheets, higher risk asset provisioning and, in some cases, regulatory restrictions on dividend distribution where prudential requirements were not fully met.” It is a conservative capital management strategy – CIS boss Commenting on the implication of the non-payment of dividends to investors, she said: “The immediate implication is a divergence in returns. Income-focused investors who rely on dividend payments may shift their preference towards banks with stronger capital positions and consistent payout records. ”For banks that suspended dividends, there could be short-term pressure on their share prices as investors reassess valuation and income expectations. ”However, if retained earnings are deployed effectively to strengthen capital and support future earnings growth, the decision could ultimately create greater long-term shareholder value.” On the implications to banks’ customers, Ahimie, said: “For customers, the impact is relatively limited in the near term. A bank’s decision not to pay dividends does not necessarily indicate financial distress. ”In many cases, it reflects a conservative capital management strategy designed to improve resilience and enhance the bank’s capacity to support lending, digital investments and business expansion. ”Stronger capital positions ultimately translate into greater confidence in the banking system.” Looking ahead, Ahimie stated: “The outlook for the banking industry remains constructive. ”As most banks already met the recapitalisation and other regulatory requirements, dividend payments are expected to become more stable and predictable. So they are likely to maintain relatively consistent distributions due to their stronger earnings capacity and capital positions.” CBN stopped the dividends – Adonri Commenting, David Adonri, Highcap Securities Limited, said: “Several banks did not pay dividends for the financial year ended December 31, 2025, because after reviewing their financial accounts, CBN was not convinced that they were strong enough to pay dividends. ”That was a stringent move by CBN to safeguard the interest of depositors notwithstanding the expectation of investors. “CBN stopped the banks affected from paying dividends because when the forbearance given banks in respect of partial provisioning for doubtful credits lapsed, the banks did not have sufficient retained profits after application of full provisioning. ”Some of the banks were faced with the need for funds to redeem their pending foreign debt obligations which would have been hampered if they dissipated their cash on dividends. “With this kind of stern regulatory action by CBN, shareholders will be forced to scrutinise the management of their banks to forestall any future threat to their dividend income. ”Banking is a delicate business. It requires stringent monitoring from regulators and shareholders to prevent abuses and failure. The action of CBN in stopping payment of dividends by some banks should boost depositors’ and investors’ confidence in the industry.” It was a regulatory push-back – Olayinka Commenting as well, Tajudeen Olayinka, Investment banker and Chartered Stockkbroker, said: “The inability of some Nigerian banks to pay dividends from their 2025 accounts arose from deliberate regulatory pushback. ”Many of the affected banks had huge final write-off from regulatory forbearance which could impact their balance sheets if they were allowed to pay dividends. ”It was CBN that refused to approve payment of dividends by these banks, by invoking its regulatory power over the banks.” While commenting on the future outlook for the industry, he said: “The industry has bright future. Most of the banks affected actually proposed to pay dividends, in spite of the need to end forbearance. ”So, it wasn’t that they didn’t have enough, CBN just felt it might appear excessively imprudent if the affected banks were allowed to pay dividends alongside huge provisions and write-off they were compelled to make. ”Some of the banks were also exposed to a huge syndicated loan default from Nestoil which they have now fully provided for. I must say that the current regulatory stance imposes discipline and prudence on Nigerian banks, which is positive for the industry and key stakeholders. Why CBN stopped some banks – Kurfi In his comments, Mallam Kasimu Kurfi, said: “The governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria has said that those banks that did not pay dividend were not able to clean their impairments and were denied to pay dividends”. He also added that one of the tier-1 banks was stopped by CBN from paying dividend because of its exposure to its foreign bank subsidiary, which was about 20% of shareholders’ funds, over the 10% limit which the CBN set in the prudential guideline. ”The banks needs to either increase their shareholders’ funds or sell some of their holdings to align with the maximum limit of 10% shareholders’ funds before they can be allowed to pay dividends to shareholders,” he said. items.title: GMA, Japan Motors launch 16th Corporate Run and Walk to support persons with visual impairment
items.description: Global Media Alliance (GMA), in partnership with Japan Motors, has launched the 16th edition of the Corporate Run and Walk, scheduled for September 21, 2026. The annual five-kilometre event promotes workplace wellness while supporting persons living with visual impairment. Held in commemoration of Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Day, the run will take place simultaneously across the Greater Accra, Ashanti, Western, and Northern Regions. Speaking at the launch, the Chief Executive Officer of Global Media Alliance, Ernest Boateng, reiterated that the initiative had over the past sixteen years, evolved into more than just a corporate fitness event. “This initiative started with a simple idea to bring Corporate Ghana together to promote health, build stronger connections and support a meaningful cause. “Today, it has become a platform that demonstrates how businesses can come together to improve lives while investing in the wellbeing of their people,” he said. Mr. Boateng explained that the event is built around the values of health, unity and inclusion, adding that 25 per cent of the proceeds from the event will once again be donated to the Ghana Blind Union to support persons living with visual impairment. The Executive Director of Lakeside Estate and Silver Star Tower, Salah Kwaku Kalmoni, described the Corporate Run and Walk as “a race of impact”, noting that the initiative has consistently prioritised social impact over competition. “For 16 years, this has never been simply a race with a charity attached to it. It has been a charity supported through a race. Every contribution helps restore dignity, independence and opportunity to persons living with visual impairment because, as we always say, mobility is freedom,” he stated. He highlighted the concept of the “Personal Best” (PB), explaining that participants are not necessarily competing against one another but are challenged to improve on their own performance. “You are not running against anyone; you are running for yourself. It is about achieving your personal best. The Corporate Run is a race of impact. We do not run only for lifestyle; we run to make an impact and contribute meaningfully to society,” he added. He said this year’s donation would go towards the provision of tandem bicycles and other mobility support to help improve the independence and mobility of persons living with visual impairment. The Marketing Manager of Japan Motors, Mabel Offei, reaffirmed the company’s commitment to the initiative, describing the sixteen-year partnership as a reflection of the company’s belief in giving back to society. “Japan Motors is proud to continue supporting this initiative because it aligns with our commitment to improving lives. “We encourage organisations and individuals to join this year’s event, knowing that every registration and every sponsorship contribute to a worthy cause while promoting healthier workplaces,” she said. Corporate institutions are encouraged to register their teams to participate in this year’s edition as part of their corporate social responsibility initiatives, while individuals are also invited to participate at a registration fee of GH¢100. Registration tickets are available at Silver Star Towers offices in Accra, Takoradi, Kumasi and Tamale. Registration forms can also be obtained from the Global Media Alliance office in Dzorwulu, Happy FM at Asylum Down, Silverbird Cinemas at Accra Mall, YFM. Participants may also register online, while enquiries and registration support are available through the event’s official social media platforms, Run Ghana, across all social media channels.

items.title: Bandits demand N500,000 from Benue farmer before harvesting crops
items.description: By Peter Duru, Makurdi A farmer in Kastina-Ala Local Government Area (LGA) of Benue State has been forced to abandon his farm after suspected bandits demanded N500,000 from him as a condition for accessing and harvesting his crops. The farmer, whose identity was not disclosed, is a resident of Mbagena Council Ward in Kastina-Ala LGA, where suspected local bandits have allegedly been terrorising residents and imposing ransom demands on members of the community. His son, a 300-level student of Benue State University, BSU, John James, disclosed this at the weekend while narrating his family’s ordeal at a capacity-building workshop on Promoting Safety and Security Rights, Accountability and Access to Justice, organised by the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project, SERAP, in Makurdi. James said his father, who combines farming with public service, was attacked in his home about two weeks ago by suspected bandits who demanded a N500,000 ransom. According to him, the attackers initially gave his father three days to raise the money, but later extended the deadline to one week after he explained that he could not immediately raise the amount because he had not harvested his farm produce. He said his father had returned home to harvest his groundnut, beniseed, soyabean and other crops in order to generate income to meet the ransom demand. James said, “About two weeks ago, terrorists invaded his compound in the night where he was sleeping alongside my mother after work. They charged him to pay a ransom of N500,000. My father pleaded with them because there was nothing at the moment. He had to plead with them for our lives because contacting the security will only worsen the situation.” He explained that while his father was struggling to raise the money, the attackers returned to the house and abducted his mother, accusing the farmer of deliberately delaying payment. James said his father was away attending a burial ceremony near Kastina-Ala town when the attackers arrived and took his mother away. He, however, said his mother was later released after one of the abductors pleaded that she should be freed because she was crying and visibly distressed. “She was freed but not without being tortured. As I talk to you now, my mother is suffering emotionally and physically from the pains she suffered in the course of the torture,” he said. According to him, his father eventually rallied friends and relatives and raised N200,000, which he delivered to the bandits at midnight on Thursday. James said the payment allowed his father to harvest only some of his crops, as the attackers insisted that he must pay the balance of N300,000 before he could return to the farm and harvest the remaining produce. “When my father returned and handed them the money, they said it was not enough, that he had to complete it to N500,000 before he would be allowed to harvest anything from his farm,” he said. The student said the continued threats had forced his father to flee the area, leaving his crops at the mercy of the bandits. “They are still threatening my father for the remaining amount, and he is on the run for fear of the unknown. He can’t go back to harvest everything now until he gets all the money,” James added. He lamented that the suspected bandits were allegedly moving freely within the community, with some of them reportedly known to residents. “These people are moving freely in our vicinity, and they are local bandits. In fact, some of them are known to the villagers because they are from the same community,” he said. James said his father’s experience was not an isolated incident, explaining that residents had suffered repeated attacks, theft and other forms of intimidation, noting that although it was the first time his father had been forced to pay ransom specifically to access his farm, he had previously been attacked, during which his money and goods were reportedly taken away. “Other villagers suffer a similar fate regularly. However, it’s the first time my father has been charged a ransom for harvest. But he had been attacked several times where his money and goods were carted away,” he said. The BSU student also raised concerns over the reluctance of residents to report attacks to security agencies, alleging that villagers who had attempted to seek police intervention were subsequently targeted by the bandits. “The villagers hardly report to police because those who attempted were killed by the bandits,” he alleged. The SERAP workshop provided a platform for community members to share experiences of insecurity and learn how to demand accountability, seek justice and better understand their rights in relation to safety and security.
